title: Crème Brûlée
subtitle: Baked vanilla custard with a caramel sugar crust
excerpt: Rich, silky baked custard perfumed with vanilla, topped with a thin disc of caramelised sugar that cracks when tapped. The standard of French restaurant desserts.

recipe.sourceNotes: Crème brûlée (burned cream) is one of the most widely debated dishes in culinary history, with France, Britain (where a similar dish called Trinity Cream or Cambridge Cream appeared at Trinity College in the seventeenth century), and Spain (crema catalana, which predates the French version) all claiming the dish. The French version became the dominant form through the prestige of French restaurant culture. The brûlée (burned) element refers to the technique of burning sugar on top of the set custard with a salamander or, in domestic kitchens, a blowtorch. The custard is richer than most, using only double cream (no milk), and the egg-to-cream ratio is high to produce the characteristic silky density. The custard must be baked in a water bath (bain-marie) at a low temperature to prevent it setting too firmly or cracking.

recipeTools.notes: Six 150 ml ramekins. A deep roasting tin for the water bath.

content.text: The custard is cooked when the edges are just set and the centre still wobbles slightly, like a jelly that has not quite set. Do not overbake: the carry-over heat of the ramekin will firm the centre as the custards cool. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours before brûléeing. The sugar crust is applied just before serving: a blowtorch produces the best result. Sprinkle 1 teaspoon of caster sugar evenly over each custard and torch in a slow circular motion from 4 to 5 cm away until the sugar bubbles, caramelises, and sets to a dark amber disc. Serve within 10 minutes.

items.preparation: plus 6 tsp for the brûlée crust

content.text: Heat the oven to 150 C / fan 130 C / gas 2. Heat the cream in a saucepan with the vanilla until steaming but not boiling. Whisk the egg yolks and sugar together in a bowl until pale. Pour the hot cream slowly over the yolks, whisking constantly.

Strain through a fine sieve into a jug. Skim off any foam. Pour into 6 ramekins. Set the ramekins in a deep roasting tin and pour boiling water into the tin to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins.

Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the edges are set but the centre wobbles gently. Remove from the water bath. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours. Sprinkle a teaspoon of caster sugar over each custard and caramelise with a blowtorch until dark amber. Serve within 10 minutes.
